meta.pageTitle: GATE CSE Algorithms Previous Year Questions – Solved PYQs

questions.text:
For constants [latex]a\geq 1[/latex] and [latex]b \gt 1[/latex], consider the following recurrence defined on the non-negative integers:

[latex]T(n) = a \cdot T \left(\dfrac{n}{b} \right) + f(n)[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct about the recurrence [latex]T(n)[/latex]?
questions.solution:
This is exactly case 1 of the Master theorem: if [latex]f(n)=O(n^{\log_b a-\epsilon})[/latex], then [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})[/latex].

The others are wrong in general: e.g. option 1 fails for a = 4, b = 2 (gives [latex]\Theta(n^2)[/latex]), and case 2 has an extra log factor ([latex]\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)[/latex]).

Answer: Option 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: if [latex]f(n)[/latex] is [latex]O(n^{\log_b(a)-\epsilon})[/latex] for some [latex]\epsilon \gt 0[/latex], then [latex]T(n)[/latex] is [latex]\Theta(n ^{\log_b(a)})[/latex].

questions.text:
Consider the string abbccddeee. Each letter in the string must be assigned a binary code satisfying the following properties:

For any two letters, the code assigned to one letter must not be a prefix of the code assigned to the other letter.
For any two letters of the same frequency, the letter which occurs earlier in the dictionary order is assigned a code whose length is at most the length of the code assigned to the other letter.

Among the set of all binary code assignments which satisfy the above two properties, what is the minimum length of the encoded string?
questions.solution:
Frequencies: a 1, b 2, c 2, d 2, e 3 (total 10).

Huffman: merge a(1) with a frequency-2 letter. To respect the tie rule (b, c, d in dictionary order), merge a with d [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3; then b + c [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4; then ad + e [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6; then 4 + 6.
Code lengths: a 3, d 3, b 2, c 2, e 2 (b [latex]\le[/latex] c [latex]\le[/latex] d True).

Length = 1[latex]\times[/latex]3 + 2[latex]\times[/latex]2 + 2[latex]\times[/latex]2 + 2[latex]\times[/latex]3 + 3[latex]\times[/latex]2 = 3 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 = 23

Answer: 23

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text:
Let G be a connected undirected weighted graph. Consider the following two statements.

S1: There exists a minimum weight edge in G which is present in every minimum spanning tree of G.
S2: If every edge in G has distinct weight, then G has a unique minimum spanning tree.

Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- S1: if several edges share the minimum weight (e.g. a triangle with all weights 1), each MST leaves out one of them, so no single minimum edge is in every MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- S2: distinct weights [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] unique MST [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: S1 is false and S2 is true

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Both S1 and S2 are true
S1 is true and S2 is false
S1 is false and S2 is true
Both S1 and S2 are false

questions.text:
An articulation point in a connected graph is a vertex such that removing the vertex and its incident edges disconnects the graph into two or more connected components.
Let T be a DFS tree obtained by doing DFS in a connected undirected graph G.
Which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- The root is an articulation point exactly when it has two or more DFS children: there are no cross edges in an undirected DFS, so its subtrees connect only through the root [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (option 1 is FALSE).
- A leaf of T: removing it leaves the rest of T connected [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] never an articulation point [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Option 4: y's subtree may have a back edge to an ancestor above u (u is an articulation point because of another subtree), giving a path from x to y that avoids u [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Root of T is an articulation point iff it has 2 or more children

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Root of T can never be an articulation point in G.
Root of T is an articulation point in G if and only if it has 2 or more children.
A leaf of T can be an articulation point in G.
If u is an articulation point in G such that x is an ancestor of u in T and y is a descendent of u in T, then all paths from x to y in G must pass through u.

questions.text:
Define [latex]R_n[/latex] to be the maximum amount earned by cutting a rod of length n meters into one or more pieces of integer length and selling them. For [latex]i > 0[/latex], let [latex]p[i][/latex] denote the selling price of a rod whose length is [latex]i[/latex] meters. Consider the array of prices:

[latex]\text{p}[1]=1,\text{p}[2]=5,\text{p}[3]=8,\text{p}[4]=9,\text{p}[5]=10,\text{p}[6]=17,\text{p}[7]=18[/latex]

which of the following statements is/are correct about [latex]R_7[/latex]?
questions.solution:
Best values: R1 = 1, R2 = 5, R3 = 8, R4 = 10 (2+2), R5 = 13 (2+3), R6 = 17, R7 = 18.

R7 = 18 is reached by:
- one piece of 7 (18)
- 6 + 1 (17 + 1)
- 2 + 2 + 3 (5 + 5 + 8)

Three different solutions, one of which has three pieces (so option 4 is false).

Answer: [latex]R_7=18[/latex] and it is achieved by three different solutions

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: [latex]R_7[/latex] is achieved by three different solutions.
[latex]R_7[/latex] cannot be achieved by a solution consisting of three pieces.
